newsitem.title: ITALY: Burundi calls for end to "devastating" sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Burundi calls for end to "devastating" sanctions.

text.p: Burundi's Prime Minister Pascal Firmin Ndimira said on Friday he backed any moves to bring peace to central Africa and appealed for sanctions imposed against Burundi after a July coup to be lifted.

Speaking at a U.N.-sponsored world food summit, Ndimira said he recognised that the Tutsi-dominated military-led regime had come to power by means that were not "strictly legal" but added that its main aim was to bring peace to Burundi.
Ndimira said the sanctions -- which he referred to as an "illegal blockade" -- had a "devastating effect" on his country and called for them to be removed.

"We hope that with this summit, the countries that have imposed the embargo will understand that our wish is to take the people of Burundi out of their distress and to bring them back to the road of peace," the prime minister said.
"We wish our neighbours...and the entire international community to help us to create the best conditions to commence this procedure towards peace by lifting the embargo."

Regional states imposed a trade and transport embargo on landlocked Burundi on July 31 in response to a coup by the army that ousted president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, a Hutu, and installed Pierre Buyoya of the minority Tutsi tribe.
Opponents have called for a restoration of the constitution and for peace talks before sanctions can be eased.
Ndimira said agricultural production should have improved this year but had not due to restrictions which prevented goods including 4,000 tonnes of fertilisers from being imported.
Gross domestic product was now $200 per capita per year, a fall of almost 15 percent over the past three years.
Ndimira said that the July 25 takeover was in response to years of political chaos and ethnic massacres.
"This event, although not strictly legal of the transitional government, should be understood as a humanitarian act, an act to rescue the Burundian people," he said.

Ndimira did not comment on the return of tens of thousands of refugees to Rwanda from eastern Zaire on Friday but said that his country was "open to any positive contribution likely to help restore peace" in Burundi and the region.
He said however that Burundi believed the multinational humanitarian intervention should focus on resolving the problems which he identified as three main issues.
-- The voluntary return of refugees to their home countries or their removal from the borders of those countries.
-- The isolation of the authors of massacres and genocide carried out against the people of Rwanda and Burundi.
-- A ban on arms trafficking in the region.
Burundi estimates 150,000 of its citizens were refugees in eastern Zaire and a similar number in Tanzania.

The U.N. Security Council agreed on Friday on a resolution to deploy a Canadian-led multinational force to bring food, water and medicines to more than a million Rwandan Hutu refugees stranded by fighting in eastern Zaire.

The United Nations said the force was still needed although Rwanda's U.N. envoy and its ambassador to Washington said its mandate was now irrelevant and resources should be used instead to help resettle the refugees inside Rwanda.
